Refresher

RBAC: role-based access

admineditorviewer

Great when roles are stable and singular.

Users are admins, editors, viewers. An admin today is an admin tomorrow. You hold one role. Works for most apps.
Where it breaks

Same user. Same app.

Adminhere 📁
Read-onlythere 📁

Think Google Drive, YouTube, Vimeo.

Permission depends on which thing, not who you are. RBAC doesn't scale to this.
Before FGA

Hand-rolled ReBAC

async function canViewDocument(user: string, id: string) {
  const doc = await db.documents.find(id);
  if (doc.ownerId === user) {
    if (!doc.blocked.includes(user)) return true;
  }
  if (doc.sharedWith.includes(user)) return true;
  const teams = await db.teams.forUser(user);
  for (const t of teams) {
    if (doc.teamIds.includes(t.id)) return true;
  }
  const org = await db.orgs.forUser(user);
  let folder = await db.folders.find(doc.folderId);
  while (folder) {
    if (folder.ownerId === user) return true;
    if (folder.orgId === org?.id) return true;
    folder = await db.folders.find(folder.parentId);
  }
  return false; // blocked? only checked for owners
}
  1. Nested ifs: owner, share list
  2. DB lookups every request
  3. Recursive folder walk
  4. blocked checked in one branch
const { allowed } =
  await fga.check({
    user,
    relation: 'can_view',
    object: `document:${id}`,
  });

Orgs, teams, folders and blocked live in the model, not in your code.

This is what we all write: owner, share list, team lookups, walking parent folders. Step 4: blocked is only checked for owners, a real bug that is easy to miss. Last press: the FGA version is one check. The rules move into the model (the schema we'll see later).

“There has to be
a better way.”

ReBAC

Relationships, not roles.

Relationship-based access control. Super clever name.
Core concepts
Typesuser, document
The kinds of things in your app.
Relationsowner, viewer
How a user can relate to an object.
Tuplesfacts:
user · relation · object
Stored data you write.
Checksquestions:
can X do Y to Z?
Answer: allowed true / false.
Types and relations = the model. Tuples = facts you write. Checks = questions you ask.
Put it all together
// model.fga: types + relations
type user
type document
  relations
    define owner: [user]
    define viewer: [user] or owner

// tuple: a fact
user:ana  owner  document:roadmap

// check: a question
can user:ana viewer document:roadmap?
→ allowed: true  (owners are viewers)
  1. Types the nouns
  2. Relations the rules
  3. Tuple the fact
  4. Check the answer
One worked example. TLA joke: it's a DSL, the OpenFGA modeling language, file ends in .fga. Ana owns the roadmap, owners are viewers, so the check is true.
Wiring it up
// 1. Write a fact (a tuple)
await fga.write({ writes: [
  { user: 'user:1', relation: 'owner', object: 'document:x' }
]});

// 2. Ask a question (a check)
const { allowed } = await fga.check({
  user: 'user:1', relation: 'viewer', object: 'document:x'
});  // → true (owners are viewers)
Model defines what can happen; you still wire it up. OpenFGA JS SDK.

Snags

Modeling is the hard part.

Like database modeling. The API calls are the easy bit.

  1. Org + team membership
  2. Folders inherit from parents
  3. Docs: owner → editor → viewer
  4. …but not blocked
model
  schema 1.1
type user
type org
  relations
    define member: [user]
type team
  relations
    define member: [user]
type folder
  relations
    define parent: [folder]
    define owner: [user, team#member]
    define editor: [user, team#member] or owner or editor from parent
    define viewer: [user, org#member] or editor or viewer from parent
type document
  relations
    define parent: [folder]
    define owner: [user]
    define blocked: [user]
    define editor: [user, team#member] or owner or editor from parent
    define viewer: [user, org#member] or editor or viewer from parent
    define can_view: viewer but not blocked
Whether you or an agent writes it, the model is the tricky part. Walk: membership, folder inheritance via parent, doc roles as computed usersets, then 'but not blocked'. Illustrative schema, not the demo's.

ReBAC scales
where RBAC fails.

Best fit: documents, folders, shared things.

Probably not 100% true, but it makes good marketing material.
Now: agents

Agents act
on behalf of
users.

Without a check, they can over-fetch: read more than the user ever could.
Screenshot: Monster Vault agent. Tool listMyVaultImages asks FGA can_view for every image before the model sees anything; decisions panel on the right.
Pattern 1

Filter before the agent sees it

// Check every retrieved image, in one call
const { result } = await fga.batchCheck({
  checks: images.map(img => ({
    user: 'user:focus', relation: 'can_view',
    object: `image:${img.id}`
  }))
});
const ok = new Set(result.filter(r => r.allowed)
  .map(r => r.request.object));
// Only these images ever reach the agent
const visible = images.filter(img => ok.has(`image:${img.id}`));
RAG-style: retrieve, then batchCheck each image before it goes into the prompt. Results aren't ordered, so match on request.object. batchCheck needs OpenFGA 1.8+.
Pattern 2

Gate every tool call

// Before the tool runs
const { allowed } = await fga.check({
  user: 'user:focus', relation: 'can_view',
  object: 'image:bo-werewolf'
});
if (!allowed) return 'Not authorized.';

Or model the agent as its own type: agent:assistant, acting for a user.
Tokens & tool access: Auth0 for AI Agents · auth0.com/ai

Agent as its own user type gets only what the user delegated. Light mention of Auth0 for AI Agents; no CIBA deep dive.
Try it · play.fga.dev · Monster Vault model
model
  schema 1.1
type user
type creature
  relations
    define viewer: [user]
type image
  relations
    define owner: [user]
    define kind: [creature]
    define can_view: owner or viewer from kind

As user:focus, seeded with
user:focus viewer creature:vampire

  1. can_view image:ana-vampire✓
  2. can_view image:bo-werewolf✗
  3. write viewer creature:werewolf
    → re-check bo-werewolf    ✓
Image tuples like creature:vampire kind image:ana-vampire need to exist in the store. Check 3: write the werewolf viewer tuple, re-run check 2, now true. No redeploy.
Demo 2

Let’s play tag.

Every tag is an
authorization check.

  • Up to 30 players
  • Guest join · no login
  • Winner gets a Lego set 🏆
phaser-colyseus-tag-stage.vercel.app
Get people joining while you show the model next.
The game’s real model
model
  schema 1.1
type user
type room
  relations
    define host: [user]
    define it: [user]
    define tagging_on: [user:*]
    define no_tagbacks: [user:*]
    define tagger: it and tagging_on
    define can_change_rules: host
type player
  relations
    define owner: [user]
    define room: [room]
    define last_tagged: [user]
    define shielded: [user:*]
    define tagback_blocked: last_tagged and no_tagbacks from room
    define can_tag: tagger from room but not (shielded or tagback_blocked)
Real model from the tag game. Next slide walks one check.
One check

Can Ana tag Bo?

await fga.check({ user: 'user:ana',
  relation: 'can_tag', object: 'player:bo' })

Ana is it · tagging on · Bo not shielded → allowed

Write user:* shielded player:bo → denied

Rules change live = writing tuples. No redeploy.
Shield and no-tagbacks are just tuples with user:* wildcards. Host flips them during the game.
Takeaways
  1. RBAC for stable roles. ReBAC when access depends on relationships.
  2. Model it. Write tuples. Ask checks.
  3. Agents get only what the user can see: filter before, check every tool call.
Three things to remember.
